entry: Indian politician, prime minister of India since May 26, 2014. A member of the [[Bharatiya Janata Party]] (BJP), he was chief minister of [[Gujarat]] from 2001 to 2014. In the 2014 general election he led the BJP to a parliamentary majority, the first for a party since 1984. His administration increased direct foreign investment and reduced spending on health care, education and social welfare. After winning a second term in 2019, it revoked the special status of [[Jammu and Kashmir (union territory)|Jammu and Kashmir]]. Critics argue that his administration was complicit in the 2002 Gujarat violence, in which over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims, were killed; an investigation authorized by the Supreme Court found no evidence to prosecute him. Critics also describe democratic backsliding under his tenure, while supporters credit his government with universal welfare delivery. According to the WHO, the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] killed 4.7 million Indians during his administration.

Ancient Egyptian king of the Early Dynastic Period, whose reign began at the end of the 4th millennium BC. Many scholars consider him the unifier of [[Egypt]] and founder of the First Dynasty. The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial siltstone artifact discovered in 1898 at Hierakonpolis, shows him wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other. He also had a more prominent presence in [[Canaan]] than his predecessors or successors. A majority of Egyptologists identify him with Menes, the first [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] according to the historian Manetho; a vigorous debate proposes Hor-Aha, his successor, instead. Necropolis sealings from Abydos are considered strong evidence that he was the first king of the First Dynasty.

Written or spoken commentary conveying a story to an [[Audience]]. A narrator, either a specific person or an unspecified literary voice, delivers information about the plot, the series of events. Narration is a required element of written stories such as [[Novel|novels]], short stories and poems, and it is optional in most other forms, such as films, plays and video games, where dialogue or visual action can carry the story. The narrative mode covers the creator's choices about the narrator, including point of view (the grammatical person used), [[Grammatical tense|tense]] (past or present) and technique, such as setting, [[Character (arts)|characters]] and structure. A common distinction is drawn between first-person and third-person narration, which Gérard Genette calls intradiegetic and extradiegetic narrative, respectively.

Emperor of Japan since May 1, 2019, the 126th monarch in the traditional order of succession. He succeeded his father, [[Akihito]], and his reign is known as the Reiwa era. Naruhito studied history at Gakushuin University and English at Merton College, Oxford. He married the diplomat Masako Owada in 1993; they have one daughter, Aiko, Princess Toshi. He has never visited Yasukuni Shrine, continuing a boycott his grandfather and father also observed over the enshrinement of convicted war criminals. He is an advocate of water policy and water conservation.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series written and illustrated by Masashi Kishimoto. It follows Naruto Uzumaki, a socially isolated [[Ninja|ninja]] who dreams of becoming Hokage, the leader of his village. Serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* from September 1999 to November 2014, it ran to 700 chapters collected in 72 volumes. The manga has sold over 250 million copies in 46 countries. Two [[Anime]] television series, produced by Pierrot and Aniplex, ran from 2002 to 2017, along with 11 animated films. It has been praised for its character development and storylines, and critics noted its references to [[Japanese mythology]] and [[Confucianism]].

Medium-sized toothed whale (*Monodon monoceros*) native to the Arctic, the only member of its [[Genus|genus]]. Males have a spiraled tusk, a protruding left canine 1.5–3.0 m long, thought to serve as a weapon, a feeding tool or a sensory organ. Narwhals are among the deepest-diving [[Cetacean|cetaceans]], reaching depths of up to 2,370 m. The [[Inuit]] have hunted them for thousands of years for meat and [[Ivory|ivory]]. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as of least concern, with an estimated 170,000 individuals, but climate change, pollution and hunting are threats.

American rapper, entrepreneur and record producer. Rooted in East Coast [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], he is regarded as one of the greatest rappers of all time. He signed with [[Columbia Records]] in 1992. His debut album, *Illmatic* (1994), regarded as one of the greatest hip-hop albums, was inducted into the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry. *It Was Written* (1996) debuted atop the Billboard 200. A highly publicized feud with [[Jay-Z]] from 2001 to 2005 helped restore his critical standing. *King's Disease* (2020) won his first Grammy Award for Best Rap Album.

American stock exchange, the largest by market capitalization and the first fully electronic stock market. Based in [[Manhattan]], New York City, it was founded in 1971 by the National Association of Securities Dealers and had no physical trading floor. As of December 31, 2024, 4,075 companies listed securities on Nasdaq. It is the primary listing for many technology companies, and [[China]] and [[Israel]] are the largest sources of its foreign listings. [[Intel]] was among the first major corporations to list its shares on the exchange.

Indian actor, primarily in [[Hindi]] films. One of the most prolific actors of Indian cinema, especially in the parallel cinema movement, he has also appeared in international productions. He has received three National Film Awards, three Filmfare Awards and the Volpi Cup for Best Actor at the Venice Film Festival. The [[Government of India]] honored him with the Padma Shri in 1987 and the Padma Bhushan in 2003. His films include *Nishant*, *Aakrosh*, *Sparsh*, *Mirch Masala* and *Ardh Satya*, and he appeared in the cult comedy *Jaane Bhi Do Yaaron* (1983).

Solution concept in non-cooperative [[Game theory|game theory]]. A set of strategies is a Nash equilibrium when no player can gain by changing their own strategy while the others keep theirs unchanged. The idea dates to 1838, when Cournot applied it to his model of competition in an oligopoly. John Nash showed that a Nash equilibrium exists, possibly in mixed strategies, for every finite game. The concept is widely used in [[Economics|economics]], and equilibria can be inefficient, as in the [[Prisoner's dilemma|prisoner's dilemma]], where mutual defection results despite a better cooperative outcome.

Capital and most populous city of [[Tennessee]], on the Cumberland River, a tributary of the [[Ohio River]]. Founded in 1779 as Fort Nashborough, it was named for Francis Nash, a general of the Continental Army in the [[American Revolutionary War]]. Its role as a river port and, in the 19th century, a railroad center fostered growth. In 1862 it became the first Confederate state capital taken by Union forces during the [[American Civil War]]. Since 1963 it has had a consolidated city-county government. It is a major center of the [[Music industry|music industry]], especially [[Country music|country music]], and is known as Music City. Its many colleges and universities earned it the nickname "Athens of the South." The city had 689,447 residents at the 2020 census.

Persian [[Polymath|polymath]], astronomer and philosopher. Born in Ṭūs, in [[Khorasan]], he was a prominent Shiʿite scholar who wrote on mathematics, engineering, philosophy, theology and the sciences. After the [[Mongols]] captured Alamūt in 1256, he entered the service of Hulagu Khan as an astrologer and helped save many libraries from destruction. He compiled the Zīj al-Khānī astronomical tables and developed an improved planetary model, and he criticized aspects of [[Ptolemy|Ptolemaic]] astronomy. He introduced the mathematical device later known as the "Ṭūsī couple." He is often credited with establishing [[Trigonometry|trigonometry]] as an independent discipline, and [[Ibn Khaldun]] regarded him as the greatest of the later non-Arab scholars. His astronomy may have influenced Copernicus. His most enduring works include *al-Akhlāq al-Nāṣiriyya* (1235).

Capital and largest city of [[The Bahamas|the Bahamas]], on New Providence island. Originally Charles Town, it was renamed Nassau in 1695 in honor of [[William III of England|King William III]]. Historically a stronghold of pirates, it was a base for privateering against the Spanish. Loyalists who settled after the [[American Revolutionary War]] eventually came to outnumber the original inhabitants. Nassau is the seat of the House of Assembly and the country's center of commerce, education, law and media. New Providence has 296,522 people, 74.26% of the national population.

German actress and former model. She has appeared in more than 60 films in Europe and the United States. Her breakthrough came with *Stay as You Are* (1978), and she won a Golden Globe Award for the title role in [[Roman Polanski]]'s *Tess* (1979). Her other films include *One from the Heart* (1982) by [[Francis Ford Coppola]], *Cat People* (1982) and *Paris, Texas* (1984) by Wim Wenders. She is the daughter of actor [[Klaus Kinski]].

American singer, [[Jazz|jazz]] pianist and actor. He formed the King Cole Trio in the late 1930s, and from 1950 he performed as a solo singer. He recorded more than 100 songs that became pop chart hits, including "Unforgettable" and "Mona Lisa." From 1956 to 1957 he hosted the [[NBC]] variety series *The Nat King Cole Show*, the first nationally broadcast television show hosted by a Black American. He was a member of the NAACP, took part in the 1963 March on Washington and regularly performed for civil rights organizations. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2000.

Israeli and American actress and filmmaker. Born in [[Jerusalem]], she moved to the [[United States]] as a child and began acting at 13 in *Léon: The Professional* (1994). She played Padmé Amidala in the *Star Wars* prequels and won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Black Swan* (2010). She later played Jane Foster in [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films. She earned a bachelor's degree in psychology from [[Harvard University]] in 2003 and co-founded the production company MountainA in 2021. She is an advocate for [[Women's rights|women's rights]].

American child actress who later played adult roles. She appeared in *Miracle on 34th Street* (1947) at age eight. Her Academy Award nominations were for *Rebel Without a Cause* (1955), *Splendor in the Grass* (1961) and *Love with the Proper Stranger* (1963). She won a Golden Globe Award for a 1979 television remake of *From Here to Eternity*. She drowned off Santa Catalina Island during a break from filming *Brainstorm* (1983), with her husband [[Robert Wagner]] and co-star [[Christopher Walken]]. In 2012 the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department listed the cause of death as "drowning and other undetermined factors."

Confederate general and slave trader. He profited from the interstate slave trade, including a slave jail in Memphis. He enlisted as a private in 1861 and rose to general during the [[American Civil War]] without prior military training, earning a reputation for aggressive [[Cavalry|cavalry]] tactics. At Fort Pillow in April 1864, Confederate forces killed many Union troops, most of them Black soldiers, after the fort had effectively ceased resistance; historians differ on whether this resulted from explicit orders. After the war he became the first Grand Wizard of the [[Ku Klux Klan]] and in 1869 ordered its dissolution.

African American religious and Black nationalist organization, founded in [[Detroit]] in 1930 by Wallace Fard Muhammad. Its teachings differ substantially from orthodox [[Islam]], and it advocates an independent African American nation-state and economic separatism. Under [[Elijah Muhammad]], who led it after Fard's disappearance in 1934, it built a business empire. [[Malcolm X]] and [[Muhammad Ali]] were prominent members. Louis Farrakhan re-established the group in 1977. Scholars classify it as a new religious movement, while critics including the Anti-Defamation League describe it as a hate group.

Public research university in [[Mexico]], based in [[Mexico City]] and known as UNAM. With more than 324,413 students, it is one of the world's largest universities, and more than 25% of scientific papers published by Mexican academics come from its researchers. Its main campus, Ciudad Universitaria, is a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage site, designed and decorated by some of Mexico's best-known architects and painters. The campus hosted the main events of the 1968 Summer Olympics and was the birthplace of the student movement of 1968. The modern university was founded on September 22, 1910, by Justo Sierra as a secular alternative to the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, founded in 1551. All Mexican Nobel laureates have been alumni of UNAM.

North American professional [[Basketball|basketball]] league of 30 teams, 29 in the United States and one in [[Canada]]. It was created on August 3, 1949, through the merger of the Basketball Association of America and the National Basketball League. The league counts its history from June 6, 1946, the founding of the Basketball Association of America. Teams play 82 regular-season games from October to April, followed by playoffs that end with the NBA Finals in June. The NBA merged with the American Basketball Association in 1976, adding four franchises. It is the second-wealthiest professional sports league by revenue, after the [[National Football League]]. The [[Boston Celtics]] have won the most championships, 18, most recently in 2024.

Nonprofit that regulates student athletics at about 1,100 schools, nearly all in the [[United States]]. Headquartered in [[Indianapolis]], it has used a three-division system since 1973, and only Division I and II schools may offer athletic scholarships. In 2021 the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] unanimously ruled that some of its restrictions on athlete compensation violate antitrust law. A 2024 settlement allowed member institutions to pay Division I athletes. Its 2022–23 revenue was $1.28 billion, 74% of it from broadcast rights to the Division I men's [[Basketball|basketball]] tournament.

Professional American football league of 32 teams, divided equally between the American Football Conference (AFC) and the National Football Conference (NFC). Founded in 1920 as the American Professional Football Association, with [[Jim Thorpe]] as its first president, it was renamed the National Football League for the 1922 season. After an agreement to merge with the rival American Football League, the first [[Super Bowl]] was held in 1967. Each team plays 17 regular-season games from early September to early January, and the playoffs culminate in the Super Bowl in early February. It is the wealthiest professional sports league in the world by revenue. The [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and [[New England Patriots]] are tied for the most Super Bowl victories, with six each.

Art museum in Trafalgar Square, central London, England. Founded in 1824 when the British government bought 38 paintings from the heirs of John Julius Angerstein, it holds more than 2,300 paintings, dating from the mid-13th century to 1900, that cover most major developments in Western painting "from [[Giotto]] to Cézanne." Private donations now account for two-thirds of the collection, and admission to the main collection is free. The present building, designed by William Wilkins, opened to the public in 1838. Its Sainsbury Wing, a 1991 extension by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, is a significant example of Postmodernist architecture in Britain. The gallery holds [[Jan van Eyck]]'s *Arnolfini Portrait*.

American monthly magazine, based in [[Washington, D.C.]]. Founded in 1888 as a scholarly journal, it began including pictures in 1905 and became known for its [[Photography|photography]]; by 1908 more than half its pages were photographs. Its distinctive format is a thick, square-bound glossy magazine with a yellow rectangular border, and it includes map supplements. During the [[Cold War]] it committed to a balanced view of the geography and people of countries beyond the [[Iron Curtain]]. The National Geographic Society owned the magazine until 2015, when National Geographic Partners gained a controlling interest. At its late-1980s peak it had 12 million subscribers in the United States. Its June 1985 cover, a portrait of a twelve-year-old Afghan girl, Sharbat Gula, by Steve McCurry, became one of its most recognizable images.
